purpose: Speaks to a patient whose hip has shortened their walks and made socks and sleep hard work. It says plainly what the practice can offer a worn hip, when a hip belongs with a surgeon instead, and what it costs, so the patient can take one step: a video call.
owner_notes: One of six Where it hurts pages, all built the same way: Is this you, What we do, What happens, What it costs, the science, three questions, then the booking band. The words on this one are about hips only.

This page tells patients that hips sit deep, so some need an image-guided injection arranged at a partner facility instead of at home. That is a statement about how the practice works, and the clinician says which applies on the call. The tag on the photo at the top reads Often treated at home for the same reason, and What it costs says the quote shows it when a partner facility is needed.
It speaks to people who want a second opinion before they see a surgeon, and it says that if a surgeon says do not wait, the practice agrees with the surgeon.
On this example the sample family doctor's referral page links here with the words Read about hip care first.
replace: What it costs: your own from and to figures replace the sample range {{site.pricing.from}} to {{site.pricing.to}}.
The closing band at the bottom: your phone number replaces the sample {{site.phone}}.
The photo at the top is licensed stock standing in; your own photo can replace it.
keep: The What we will not promise card: the treatment is not FDA-approved for hips and is investigational, results vary, and a hip that has lost its joint space or shape is a surgical hip that goes back to the specialist with notes.
The line in Who it tends to suit that candidacy is a clinical decision made on the video call, with imaging.
The answer that says if your surgeon says do not wait, the practice agrees with your surgeon.
The small print at the bottom: statements not evaluated by the FDA, individual results vary, and the California notice unless your own lawyer confirms it does not apply.

top.say: The top of the page puts hip trouble in everyday words, shorter walks, socks and sleeping on that side, and offers one button, Book a video call.

is-this-you.say: Is this you lists five situations a hip patient will recognise, ending with wanting an honest second opinion before seeing a surgeon.

what-we-do.say: What we do is three cards: the treatment in plain words, who it tends to suit, and what the practice will not promise for a hip.

what-happens.say: What happens sets out three steps: a video call, a written plan and price, then treatment and follow-ups.

cost.say: What it costs gives the range for a plan for one area, {{site.pricing.from}} to {{site.pricing.to}} on this example, which is a sample. It adds that the quote says so if treatment needs a partner facility.

the-science-if-you-want-it.say: The science, if you want it, links to three short guides, including one on who is and is not a candidate.

questions.say: Questions answers three things hip patients ask: whether a hip can be treated at home, whether a replacement date makes it too late, and how soon they would know if it helped.

questions.q: What is the Hips page for?
alt: Why is there a page just for hips?
What does the Hips page do?
questions.say: The Hips page speaks to someone whose walks keep getting shorter and who can no longer sleep on that side. It says what your practice can offer a worn hip, and when a hip belongs with a surgeon instead. It ends with one step, a video call.

questions.q: Where does the Hips page say whether a hip can be treated at home?
alt: Why does the Hips page mention a partner facility?
Does the site say hips are treated at home?
questions.say: In two places: the first card under What we do, and the first answer under Questions. It says a nurse practitioner comes to the home, but some hips need an image-guided injection arranged at a partner facility instead. The clinician says which applies on the call, before anything is booked or paid for.

questions.q: Why does the Hips page start with socks and sleep, and not with the science?
alt: Why is the science at the bottom of the page?
Why does the page open with Is this you?
questions.say: Because a patient looks for themselves first. The page opens with everyday situations in their own words: shorter walks, socks, sleeping on that side. The science sits near the bottom, as three short guides for anyone who wants to read before deciding.

questions.q: What do I change on the Hips page?
alt: What do I replace on the hip page?
questions.say: Your price range in the What it costs part and your phone number beside the booking button at the bottom. Both are samples on this example. The photo at the top is a stock stand-in you can swap for your own.

questions.q: What is the California notice at the bottom of the Hips page?
alt: Do I need the California notice?
Can I take the California notice off?
questions.say: It is a notice California law requires from practices that offer stem cell therapies that are not FDA-approved. It sits in the small print on every Where it hurts page. A practice outside California can switch it off, and your own lawyer confirms that before launch.

questions.q: Do the referral pages link to the Hips page?
alt: How does a patient sent by their doctor reach the Hips page?
questions.say: Yes. On this example the family doctor's referral page, which is a sample, has a link that says Read about hip care first, and it opens the Hips page.

questions.q: Should I cancel my hip replacement?
alt: I already have a surgery date for my hip. Is it too late to try this?
questions.say: I can't advise you on that; it is a question for your surgeon. The page says that if the date is elective and your surgeon says waiting is safe, there is a window to try a non-surgical option first. If your surgeon says do not wait, the practice agrees with your surgeon.

questions.q: What would it cost for my hip?
alt: Where is the price on the Hips page?
questions.say: The part called What it costs gives a range for a plan for one area: {{site.pricing.from}} to {{site.pricing.to}}, which is a sample on this example site. Care is paid out of pocket. A clinician decides on the call what, if anything, makes sense, and your written quote says so if treatment needs a partner facility.
